Observed learning · 2026-10-27 · two descriptive seed cohorts

Franka cable lift: four learning backends

Stock RSL-RL PPO, native CUDA PPO, pristine authors’ Torch FlashSAC AMP and native CUDA FlashSAC AMP on the same Isaac Lab cable task.

What was measured. Eight fresh training processes each collect 49,152,000 environment transitions; 72 common deterministic evaluations reuse the same 128 physical states and goals. The plots and table retain every seed and saved checkpoint, including failures. There is no preregistered population task-solved threshold, no confidence interval and no assumed policy-quality equivalence.

Observed findings. Across these two seed cohorts, final mean ever-goal / final-hold fractions were 95.70% / 89.06% for stock PPO and 92.19% / 82.81% for native PPO. Native PPO used 5.8% less mean training-plus-evaluation wall time (31.06 versus 32.99 minutes); per-seed goal and hold outcomes differ, as shown below. Both FlashSAC implementations recorded zero goal and lift outcomes at every saved checkpoint in both seeds. Native FlashSAC used 13.6% less mean training-plus-evaluation wall time (34.51 versus 39.95 minutes). These are descriptive observations, not evidence of equivalent policy quality or an isolated kernel-speed effect.

Physical diagnostics at the final checkpoint

Lift means the middle cable segment exceeded 5.0 cm in height at least once. Height gain is the mean per-episode maximum middle height minus its initial height. Final distance is from segment 6 to the goal. Failure is one minus the clean-timeout fraction: any task termination, including one coinciding with a timeout. Every scored first episode ended within 150 steps.

Execution costs

Methods and limits

Two distinct NVIDIA L40S allocations each execute one four-backend seed cohort. The registered Isaac-Lift-Cable-Franka state task uses 69 observations and 8 joint-space actions, without adapter-added clipping. Stock training rewards, resets, geometry, actuators and gravity/action-rate curricula remain intact. The comparison uses 1,024 environments and 2,000 iterations instead of the stock task's 8,192 environments and 3,000 iterations; the stock PPO horizon of 24 is retained. The Newton MJWarp rigid solver and VBD cable solver exchange rigid-body proxies. Coupled physics capture and native learning capture are separate graphs; Torch observations, rewards, reset logic and collection remain outside a single combined graph.

The stock arm target is current joint position + 0.03 × action. SAC's tanh limits each arm target offset to ±0.03 rad per control step; unclipped PPO can request larger offsets. The gripper separately clips to [−1,1] and maps to joint limits. Evaluation action RMS describes deterministic commands, not training exploration; a raw action magnitude ≥1 does not by itself mean actuator saturation. Whether this control-range difference affects learning is untested.

Every evaluation uses full cable gravity (−9.81 m/s²) and the final action-rate penalty (−0.1), including checkpoint 0. The stock Franka arm retains its gravity-disabled setting; full gravity here refers to the world/cable. The canonical fixture includes robot/cable poses and velocities, actuator targets, command goals/timers, action and clock buffers, gravity and sticky reward state. Physical and manager hashes and the raw initial observation hash must match at every checkpoint. Public scene writes cold-reset Newton solver history; no historical solver-cache, simulator or global-RNG trajectory continuation is claimed.

PPO retains the stock [256,128,64] ELU models and actual RSL-RL observation normalization. The native adapter updates those same normalizers once after the full PPO update; their state is checkpointed and frozen during evaluation. Stock Torch PPO allows TF32, while native PPO uses strict FP32 dense math. Official FlashSAC uses compiled Torch FP16 AMP; native FlashSAC uses FP16 dense operands with FP32 outputs/accumulation, master weights, adjoints and optimizer state. AMP rounding, scaler behavior and stochastic trajectories can differ.

Initial model states are matched within the PPO pair and within the FlashSAC pair for each seed. Different algorithms retain their different architectures and objectives: PPO γ=0.98, FlashSAC γ=0.99. The shared FlashSAC recipe uses one-step returns, 10M replay, 100,000-transition warmup, batch 2048 and a fixed 12,800-update learning-rate decay; this is an adaptation, not an authors-published cable recipe.

All final SAC continuation checkpoints retain the full replay and optimizer state; export costs remain in checkpoint, training-loop and whole-process wall. Native replay stores one additional FP32 discount per transition. Actual optimizer completions and AMP skips are audited from checkpoint payloads, not inferred from attempted calls. Smoke runs prove checkpoint restoration after deliberate model/optimizer perturbation and finite continued updates; they are excluded from production quality curves.

Identical MDP settings do not imply identical collection costs: learned trajectories and reset frequencies can differ. Whole-run elapsed time includes those effects and cannot isolate the contribution of learning kernels.

Seed 0 runs the four recipes forward on allocation A; seed 1 runs them in reverse on allocation B. These two cohorts do not fully balance position or predecessor effects. Seed, allocated GPU and chronology vary together; smokes and earlier workers warm shared compiler caches. A smaller elapsed time must be interpreted alongside physical task outcomes.

Provenance and credit

Schulman et al., Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms (2017); actual RSL-RL 5.5.1 implementation. Kim et al., FlashSAC: Fast and Stable Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for High-Dimensional Robot Control (2026); pristine official source (Holiday Robotics, MIT). Native FlashSAC is a RoboLearn adaptation retaining the authors’ architecture and losses. The measured RoboLearn source includes the native learners and comparison harness. Task/simulator credit: upstream Isaac Lab baseline, the measured Isaac Lab source with the shared-stream repair and Newton.
